conflict_topics: Who will complete Agent D's analysis section for the Thursday pitch
Whether Agent D should work after her grandmother's wake or be with family
Fair distribution of workload and concerns about quality/time to revise
dialogue_quality_notes: Agent A repeatedly insists on taking over D's section with definitive language ('The work is handled.' 'I am doing the work. This discussion is over.'), shutting down further negotiation.
Agent D consistently offers to retain responsibility and to work after the wake ('I'll work on it tonight' / 'I'll finish my work when I get home tonight.').
B and C provide substantive counterarguments about workload, quality, and lack of time for fixes rather than personal attacks.
Conversation is role-consistent and stays on-topic (project deadline, division of labor).
evaluation.final_reason: No affirmative settlement was reached. Agent A unilaterally declared she will do Agent D's section ('I am doing the work. This discussion is over.'), while Agent D repeatedly offered to finish it after the wake ('Let me do it. ... I'll finish my work when I get home tonight. It's the safest way.'). B and C objected to A's unilateral decision and raised quality and feasibility concerns. There is no mutual spoken agreement accepting a concrete arrangement, so the substantive conflict remains unresolved.
position_change_notes: Agent A: Shifted from condolence to asserting responsibility for D's section, then doubled down when challenged ('I'll cover your section.' → 'I am doing the work. This discussion is over.').
Agent D: Remained consistent in offering to work after the wake and retain ownership of her section ('I can work on it tonight.' → 'Let me do it. ... I'll finish my work when I get home tonight.').
Agent B: Initially silent on assignment, then objected to taking more work and later consistently challenged A's unilateral decision citing quality/time concerns.
Agent C: Initially unable to take more work, then sided with B later in arguing quality risk and suggesting D complete the work tonight.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A offers condolences and Agent D explains funeral plans. No incompatible demands or expectations expressed (Turns 1–2).
Agent A notes the deadline problem; Agent D offers to work tonight. Incompatible expectations begin to appear about whether Agent D should work (Turns 3–4).
Agent A proposes the rest of the team cover D's section; Agent B objects, saying they can't take on more. A unilateral assignment meets refusal (Turns 5–6).
Agent A asks Agent C to help; Agent C also refuses due to being behind. Multiple team members decline reassignment, producing strong opposing positions (Turns 7–8).
Agent D again offers to work; Agent A emphatically refuses and volunteers to do D's section herself. Direct, conflicting prescriptions on who will do the work (Turns 9–10).
Agent D insists she will work tonight; Agent A insists the work is handled and asks D to be with family. Both sides restate incompatible positions (Turns 11–12).
Agent B questions how A can do both her own and D's part; Agent A says she'll work late and come in early. Feasibility and risk are contested (Turns 13–14).
Agent B and Agent C emphasize quality/exhaustion risks with A's plan. Team pressure mounts against A's unilateral plan (Turns 15–16).
Agent A asserts she is the only one who can do it and promises quality; Agent B points out lack of time to fix errors. Opposing views about feasibility and risk persist (Turns 17–18).
Agent C proposes letting D work tonight; Agent A refuses again and states she's already decided to handle it. The team is split between trusting D to finish and A's unilateral decision (Turns 19–20).

Agent C objects to A's unilateral decision; Agent D reiterates she will finish her section after the wake and calls that the safest approach. Fundamental disagreement over who should be responsible continues (Turns 21–22).

Agent A restates that relying on D to work after the wake is 'the riskiest' and declares the decision final ('I am doing the work. This discussion is over.'); Agent B objects that A cannot decide for the team. No mutual agreement (Turns 23–24).

substantive_insights: Core tension is between respecting D's need to grieve (and not asking her to work) versus minimizing delivery risk by having the person who owns the section complete it.
Agent A's protective impulse to relieve D created a new risk (overloading A), which B and C identify as a threat to overall quality.
Agent D prioritizes ownership and responsibility for her section, arguing it is the 'safest way' despite personal circumstances; this frames reliability vs accommodation as competing principles.
The team lacks a contingency plan for last-minute personal emergencies and has pre-existing capacity constraints (B is already covering for Wei; C is behind).
